title: Encrypted Channel
summary: An encrypted channel is command and control traffic that the malware itself encrypts, rather than relying only on whatever protection the carrier protocol already provides. The operator selects an algorithm, generates or embeds a key, and encrypts the payload before it is placed inside the transport. The plaintext instruction therefore never appears on the wire, so content inspection and simple signatures fail. What remains observable is metadata: the destination, the timing and regularity of the connections, the size of the encrypted blobs, and whether the traffic follows a recognised standard such as TLS (Transport Layer Security) or a custom format. A defender distinguishes hostile encryption from normal encryption by the context around it, because a process with no business talking to the internet, or a session whose certificate and handshake match no known service, is suspicious even when the bytes are unreadable. Keys that are encoded in a sample or a configuration file are themselves a weakness that an analyst can use during reverse engineering.

beginner.definition: Encryption turns readable data into a secret code. An encrypted channel means the attacker's commands and replies are sent in that secret code. Only the attacker's software can read them. This hides what the traffic says, even when someone can see the traffic.
beginner.whyItMatters: Many security tools work by reading network content. If that content is encrypted, those tools see nothing useful. The attacker's instructions stay private, including orders to steal files. Normal websites also use encryption, so you cannot block it all. You must judge by the behaviour of the process, not only by the bytes.
howItWorks: The malware carries an encryption routine and a key, or it receives a key.
Before sending anything, it scrambles the command into unreadable data that is called ciphertext.
The ciphertext travels inside a normal looking connection to the control server.
The control server decrypts the message with the matching key and reads it.
Replies are encrypted in the same way before they travel back to the host.
Analysts see the connection and its size, but not the message inside it.
beginner.example: Imagine a shared flat where notes are left on the kitchen table. Anyone can read a plain note. Now suppose two flatmates write in a private code that only they understand. The notes still sit on the table, and the paper still looks the same. You can see that notes are passing, but not what they say. Encrypted channels work like that code. You cannot read the note, so you watch who writes, how often, and how large the notes are.
takeaways: Encryption hides the content but not the destination, timing or size.
Judge encrypted traffic by the process and the host behind it.
A stored key can let an analyst decrypt captured traffic later.

objectives: Describe what an encrypted channel is and why an attacker would use one.
Explain why content inspection alone fails against encrypted traffic.
List the metadata that remains visible in an encrypted session.
Explain how a stored key can support later analysis of captured traffic.
Explain the difference between this technique and its two sub-techniques.
